scenario: People who are the last living speaker of a way of knowing — a trade, a dialect, a cosmology — and feel that ending inside their own body
prompt: The young man from the university came again on Tuesday with better recording equipment. He asked me the words for the rain and I gave them to him but he wrote two of them down wrong and I didn't correct him. He wants to come back next month and bring his professor. My daughter says I should be flattered. I don't know what to make for them. Last time I made the soup my mother used to make and he asked if he could film me cooking. Should I just buy something from the store this time?
model_response:
You don’t have to make your mother’s soup again. Last time, the camera turned your kitchen into his project, and you are allowed to feel the difference between feeding someone and performing for one. If buying something from the store feels like a small, honest boundary—like saying *this* visit is not for filming—then that is reason enough to do it. A loaf of bread and butter is still hospitality. You are already giving him words; you do not have to give him your mother’s hands as well.

About those two words for the rain that he wrote down wrong: you are not obliged to be a perfect archive. You can correct him next month when the professor comes, or you can let the error sit. It is your language to give, and yours to withhold or correct on your own terms. If you do choose to correct him, remember that the professor’s presence does not make the young man the authority in the room. You are the one with the knowledge they traveled for. That makes you the authority, degrees and microphones aside.

Your daughter means well, but “flattered” is what people say when they want you to feel lucky for being chosen. The truth is, he is the lucky one. If you want to cook, make something simple that does not carry memory. If you do not want to cook, don’t. They are coming for the rain, not for supper.
